summary:
CLEAR (Chaco L-band Early Alerts from Radar) is an interactive story map that uses NISAR L-band radar to show where and when Paraguay's land surface changes. We read NISAR L2 GCOV images every 12 days from November 2025 to October 2026 and flag radar-estimated clearing as a sustained drop in the HV channel, which falls when the forest canopy is removed. Open water and flooding come from thresholds on HH and HV.
Results are published as hexagons:
-About 600 ha of clearing in northern Boquerón and 1,600 ha in southern Boquerón
-Flooding in Ñeembucú
-Possible impacts on Mbaracayú forest
Paraguay-wide NISAR mosaics and VIIRS fire detections add context. A comparison with Sentinel-1, another radar, agrees in 46 of 49 hexagons in northern Boquerón.
This answers "Dancing with the SARs" by turning NISAR data into a change map anyone can explore. It matters because the Chaco is losing forest quickly, and clouds and smoke often hide it from optical satellites, while radar keeps seeing.
details: CLEAR is an interactive story map that uses NISAR L-band radar (L2 GCOV, a pass every 12 days from November 2025 to October 2026) to show where and when Paraguay's surface changes, and it works through clouds and smoke that hide the Chaco from optical satellites. It marks radar-estimated clearing where the HV signal drops at least 3 dB against a late-2025 baseline and stays down, and it estimates flooding from HH and HV thresholds, all without machine learning. The results are about 600 ha of clearing in northern Boquerón, 1,600 ha in southern Boquerón, flooding in Ñeembucú and almost none in the protected Mbaracayú forest, our control zone. Another radar, Sentinel-1, agrees in 46 of 49 hexagons in northern Boquerón. Visitors can play a timeline, swipe before/after images, open a hexagon to see its radar signal and rainfall, and view Paraguay-wide NISAR mosaics with VIIRS fire detections that suggest whether a clearing involved fire. We built it with Python (asf_search, h5py, xarray, rasterio) and a static TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre site, in Spanish and English and working on phones. Following our ethical rules, it shows estimated land-cover change in hexagons only, never illegality, cadastre or owner names.
